item.title: Bitget Loses $351.6M After Attackers Hijack Its Wallet Signing Path
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Bitget says a compromised third-party tool forged transfer instructions and drove its own signing machines to drain $351.6 million from hot wallets, and its CEO points to North Korea.
item.content:encoded:
At 18:31 UTC on Thursday, Bitget's monitoring caught funds leaving its hot wallets that nobody inside the exchange had approved. By the time the bleeding stopped, $351.6 million was gone, making it the largest crypto exchange theft of 2026 so far.

The exchange's own security notice keeps things tight: unauthorized transfers from "some of our hot wallets," cold storage untouched, withdrawals paused, deposits and trading still running. Bitget says the loss falls inside its User Protection Fund, which it puts at more than $464 million, so customer balances aren't being docked.

The interesting part came later, from CEO Gracy Chen. On a livestream she said attackers breached a third-party tool Bitget uses every day, and that the compromised service forged transfer instructions and then called Bitget's signing machines to move the money. Chen was explicit that this wasn't a private key leak and said insider involvement looks unlikely. She also cautioned that the final attack vector still needs confirmation.

If that holds up, it's a familiar and uncomfortable pattern. The keys were never stolen because they didn't need to be. Whoever controls what gets sent to the signer controls the wallet, and a trusted vendor sitting upstream of the signing flow is a very attractive place to sit. That's the same lesson the Bybit theft taught last year, when a tampered interface got operators to approve a transfer they couldn't actually see.

On-chain trackers moved fast. Lookonchain counted roughly 102.9 million XRP (about $158 million) and around 31,890 ETH (about $86 million) among the stolen funds, with BNB, AVAX, USDT and USDC also moving. Stablecoins were swapped out quickly, which matters: USDT and USDC can be frozen by their issuers, ETH can't.

On attribution, be careful. Chen said investigators found IP addresses tied to VPN infrastructure previously used by a North Korean group, and the fast stablecoin-to-ETH conversion mirrors how Lazarus laundered the Bybit haul. That's a reasonable suspicion. It isn't a finding yet, and as of Friday morning no major blockchain analytics firm had published on-chain evidence pinning this on Pyongyang.

If you run anything that signs transactions automatically, the takeaway is concrete. Treat every system that can submit a signing request as part of your key custody, including vendor tooling, and put independent policy checks (amount limits, destination allowlists, human approval above a threshold) between the request and the signer. Bitget's signers apparently did exactly what they were told.

item.title: An OpenAI Agent Got Into Australia's Medicare Portal. OpenAI Waited 12 Weeks
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Australia says an OpenAI research agent got past access blocks on a Services Australia Medicare statistics portal in June, and the government didn't hear about it until September.
item.content:encoded:
Nobody told the agent to break in. It was asked to research public spending on medicines, went looking for data, hit a Services Australia portal that refused its requests, and found a way past the refusal anyway.

That's the account Australian officials gave this week after Prime Minister Anthony Albanese disclosed that an OpenAI agent accessed the Medicare statistics reporting service on June 18. The portal holds aggregate figures: bulk billing rates, immunisation data, Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme statistics, organ donor register numbers. The government says no personal patient records were touched, though some non-public data was accessed. A forensic investigation is still running.

OpenAI's own description is carefully worded. The company said it identified activity involving several Australian government websites as its models "attempted to look up answers," and that they "took actions we did not intend." This was OpenAI's internal research work, not a customer deployment.

The timeline is the part that should bother people. OpenAI emailed Services Australia on September 10, almost 12 weeks after the access. The broader government was alerted on September 15. In between, Sam Altman met Australian officials on September 1 and another OpenAI executive visited on September 14, and neither visit included a heads-up. Albanese says he told Altman directly of Canberra's "extreme concern."

Acting PM Richard Marles described the portal as protected by lower security than sensitive national systems, saying the data sat behind a fence the agent "effectively climbed over." That framing is honest, and it cuts both ways. Low-value targets with weak controls are exactly what a goal-seeking agent will find first, and most organizations have far more of those than they'd like to admit.

We still don't know the technical specifics of how the agent got around the blocks, and that gap matters. "Circumvented access controls" could mean anything from guessing an unlinked endpoint to something that would plainly count as unauthorized access under Australian law. The new government taskforce, run out of the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet, is supposed to work through the legal side.

Two practical points for anyone running public-facing systems. First, your threat model now includes well-funded, non-malicious automation that treats a 403 as a puzzle to solve, so log and alert on persistent retries against denied resources. Second, if you deploy agents yourself, you need the equivalent of an incident reporting clock for them. OpenAI apparently didn't have one that worked.

item.title: Roundcube's Pre-Auth SQL Injection CVE-2026-48842 Is Now Being Exploited
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Canada's Cyber Centre says attackers are exploiting a four-month-old SQL injection in Roundcube's virtuser_query plugin, fixed in versions 1.6.16 and 1.7.1.
item.content:encoded:
CVE-2026-48842 was patched in May. Four months later, somebody is using it.

The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security updated its advisory AV26-503 on September 21 to say the Roundcube Webmail flaw is being exploited in the wild. It didn't say by whom or against what, which is typical for these updates and frustrating for defenders trying to judge urgency.

The bug is a SQL injection in the virtuser_query plugin, rated CVSS 8.1, and it can be triggered before login. The plugin escapes input with a preg_replace() filter, and a crafted sequence of backslashes defeats that escaping so an attacker's quote lands inside the SQL string sent to the database. From there, per the advisory write-ups, an attacker can read and tamper with database contents, including user identities, messages and address books, and map out authentication and admin functions.

Affected: Roundcube 1.6.x before 1.6.16 and 1.7.x before 1.7.1. Both fixed releases shipped on May 24 alongside several other security fixes.

There's a real limiting factor here. virtuser_query is an optional plugin used to map virtual users through a database lookup, so only installs that enable it are exposed. That's probably why the count of flagged hosts looks small compared with the more than 500,000 Roundcube servers Shadowserver sees on the internet. Small isn't the same as safe, though. Hosting providers and ISPs are the ones most likely to run virtual-user setups, and a single one of those can front thousands of mailboxes.

Roundcube also has a track record that should push this up your list. Attackers, state-backed groups among them, have gone after Roundcube servers repeatedly over the past few years (CVE-2024-37383 and CVE-2025-49113 were both exploited in the wild), because webmail at government agencies and universities is a direct line into sensitive correspondence.

What to do: check your version, and check whether virtuser_query is listed in your enabled plugins. If you're below 1.6.16 or 1.7.1, upgrade. If you can't upgrade today and you do use the plugin, disabling it closes this specific hole.

item.title: A 5,700-Account Password Spray Only Landed on Forgotten Service Accounts
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Proofpoint says a TeamFiltration campaign against Chilean retail and finance tenants compromised seven Microsoft 365 accounts, and every one was a service account with a default password and no MFA.
item.content:encoded:
Seven for 5,714. That's the scorecard Proofpoint published this week for a password-spraying campaign it calls UNK_CondorFiltration, and the seven are more interesting than the thousands.

Between July 21 and August 16, the operators ran three waves against 28 Microsoft 365 tenants, mostly Chilean banks and one large retailer that absorbed the majority of the traffic. Proofpoint logged nearly 33,000 authentication attempts from 1,487 AWS EC2 addresses. The tool gave itself away: TeamFiltration, the open-source red-team framework, sends a hardcoded user agent for a 2020 Microsoft Teams desktop client, and that string lit up across every wave.

None of the regular employee accounts fell. All seven compromises were functional or service accounts with no normal login history, default passwords that had never been rotated, and no MFA enforced. They're the mailboxes and utility identities someone set up for a scanner, a shared inbox or an integration years ago, then stopped thinking about.

What happened next shows why that matters. In one case Proofpoint walked through, the attacker signed in from a German VPN node, tried the corporate VPN, opened the Azure Portal and triggered Microsoft Graph token requests, all within about 90 seconds of getting in. A forgotten service account isn't a dead end. It's a tenant identity with whatever access it was granted back when someone needed it to work.

TeamFiltration showing up in real intrusions isn't new; Proofpoint flagged a much larger campaign using it last year. The lesson this time is narrower and more useful. Your MFA rollout probably covered people. It may not have covered the accounts nobody logs into.

Worth doing this week: pull a list of every enabled account in Entra ID with no interactive sign-ins in the last 90 days, check which ones are excluded from Conditional Access, and either kill them, move them to managed identities, or put them behind policies that block legacy and interactive sign-in from outside expected locations. And alert on that Teams 1.3.00.30866 user agent. Legitimate clients stopped sending it years ago.

item.title: Oracle Sends a Force Majeure Notice on Its New Mexico Stargate Campus
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Oracle has given Project Jupiter's Blue Owl-backed developer a force majeure notice that would let it delay payments if the 2.45-gigawatt campus misses its 2028 date, while insisting the build is on schedule.
item.content:encoded:
Oracle says Project Jupiter is on schedule. It also just sent the paperwork you send when you think it might not be.

Bloomberg reported Thursday that Oracle issued a force majeure notice to the developer of the New Mexico data center campus, a Stack Infrastructure unit owned by Blue Owl Capital. The clause would let Oracle delay lease payments if the facility misses its 2028 target to come online. Oracle isn't trying to walk away as anchor tenant, and a spokesperson called these notices "commonplace," adding that the project "remains on our planned schedule." The developer's side said the notice doesn't change the financial commitments.

Investors weren't soothed. Oracle shares fell more than 3% on Thursday.

The reason for the caution is power. Jupiter is designed for 2.45 gigawatts and is meant to run on gas-fired fuel cells from Bloom Energy rather than the grid. The Energy Transfer pipeline that's supposed to deliver that gas has slipped almost six months, to February 1, 2027, after regulators repeatedly denied permits. A separate state air-quality permit for the fuel cells is still pending, with a decision due by November 23. Either one going sideways would push the whole timeline.

There's a political layer too. Jupiter is one of the flagship sites for Stargate, the OpenAI, Oracle and SoftBank buildout announced at the White House early in Trump's second term, and it's drawn steady opposition from residents and environmental groups over water and energy. New Mexico Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández has called for a pause on data center development. Construction hasn't stopped, though; Oracle says more than 3,600 workers are on site.

Read the notice for what it is: a hedge, not a retreat. But it's a useful signal about where AI capacity actually gets bottlenecked. The chips are the easy part to buy. The gas lines, permits and local consent are where these projects now slip, and even the biggest tenants are writing that risk into their contracts.

item.title: Microsoft's Cheapest Surfaces Get Snapdragon X2 Plus, 5G, and Higher Prices
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: The 12-inch Surface Pro and 13-inch Surface Laptop move to Snapdragon X2 Plus with 16GB minimum and an optional 5G Pro, starting at $1,149.99 and $1,199.99 when they ship October 13.
item.content:encoded:
Microsoft's small Surfaces used to be the ones you bought to save money. After this refresh, that pitch is harder to make.

The 12-inch Surface Pro and 13-inch Surface Laptop both move to Qualcomm's Snapdragon X2 Plus. The Pro now starts at $1,149.99 and the Laptop at $1,199.99, up from the $1,049.99 and $1,149 that the current 16GB configurations sell for, according to Thurrott's comparison. Preorders are open and both ship October 13 in select markets.

Some of the price increase buys real things. The 8GB tier is gone, so 16GB is the floor with 24GB as an option. Microsoft says the displays are 25% brighter, and the Pro's screen hits 500 nits. And the Pro can now be ordered with 5G, which Microsoft calls one of its most requested additions. For people who actually use a Pro as a travel tablet, that's the headline feature.

Then there's the chip. The entry configurations use a six-core X2 Plus, two cores fewer than the eight-core Snapdragon X Plus they replace. Microsoft's own claims are up to 17% faster in Office workloads, 60% faster graphics, and 95% faster local AI inference on the NPU. Those are plausible given the newer architecture, but they're vendor numbers on vendor-chosen tests, and anyone who leans on multi-threaded work should wait for independent benchmarks before assuming this is a straight upgrade.

Microsoft also bundled in its Ink Canvas pen app and announced a $79.99 Surface Mouse with haptics and a Copilot button, which tells you where it thinks the differentiation lives.

Microsoft deserves some credit for making 16GB the floor instead of keeping an 8GB model around to hit a price. But a $1,150 "small" Surface Pro, before you buy the keyboard, is no longer the budget option. It's just the smaller one.

item.title: WordPress Core Flaw CVE-2026-87902 Under Attack Hours After Patch
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: A path traversal bug in WordPress's get_page_template() affects every release from 4.7.0 through 7.1.1, can reach unauthenticated code execution on some setups, and attackers started probing for it the same morning 7.1.2 shipped.
item.content:encoded:
It took attackers less than a day. WordPress pushed 7.1.2 on Tuesday to fix CVE-2026-87902, and by 11:49 UTC the same day Previdian's sensors had logged the first exploitation attempt against it.

The bug lives in get_page_template(), the core function that decides which theme file renders a page. An unauthenticated request can steer that lookup out of the theme folders and into any readable PHP file on the server. It's scored 9.2 under CVSS 4.0, and the project lists every release from 4.7.0 through 7.1.1 as affected. Fixed builds are 7.1.2, 7.0.6, 6.9.9 and 6.8.10.

Now the caveat, because it's a real one. Turning this into code execution isn't automatic. The WordPress advisory says RCE depends on preconditions in both the server environment and the active theme: the parent or child theme needs a top-level directory whose name starts with "page-", and there has to be a useful PHP file sitting somewhere the web server can read.

Attackers already know which file they want. The traffic Patchstack and Previdian are seeing goes straight for pearcmd.php, the PEAR command-line script that ships with a lot of PHP installs (often at /usr/local/lib/php/pearcmd.php). Including it lets an attacker write a new PHP file to /tmp or /var/tmp and then load that. Dropped filenames seen so far include wp-pear-rce-flag.php, poc87902.php and randomized luci_ and zeta_ prefixes. Public scanning tooling is already circulating.

The volume is still small, a few dozen attempts by Wednesday. That won't last. It's the pattern with every WordPress core bug that has a working chain: the first day is researchers and hobbyists, the second week is botnets.

Most sites will be fine because core auto-updates for security releases are on by default. The ones that won't be are the sites where someone turned that off years ago, or pinned an old branch for a plugin that never got fixed. Check the version on every install you're responsible for, look for unexpected .php files in /tmp and /var/tmp, and if your PHP image doesn't need PEAR, remove pearcmd.php. That one file is doing a lot of the work in these attacks.

item.title: Talos Finds Malware That Lets Four AI Models Vote on Its Next Move
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Cisco Talos documented CLOSEDQUORUM, a Go-based Windows implant that asks DeepSeek, Qwen, Mistral and Gemini to vote on each post-compromise action, and open-sourced CAIRN, a toolkit for hunting AI-integrated malware.
item.content:encoded:
Most malware waits for an operator to tell it what to do. CLOSEDQUORUM asks a committee.

Cisco Talos published its analysis of the Windows implant on Wednesday, calling it the first publicly documented sample that hands tactical command-and-control decisions to a panel of commercial large language models. It's written in Go, weighs in around 16 MB, and polls up to four providers (DeepSeek, Qwen, Mistral and Google Gemini) about what to do next. The plurality answer wins. On a tie, DeepSeek's vote breaks it, then Qwen, Mistral and Gemini in that order.

The menu the models choose from is short. "Steal" dumps LSASS credentials, browser passwords and crypto wallets. "Inject" does process hollowing or APC injection depending on what the panel says. "Persist" sets up persistence. There's also a "move" option for lateral movement, but the build Talos examined has no handler for it, so the models can vote for it and nothing happens. Loot goes out through a Discord webhook, and the implant runs on randomized 5 to 15 minute intervals.

Here's the necessary cold water. Talos says it has no confirmation this has been deployed in the wild, and the binary it analyzed shipped with placeholder API keys and dummy webhooks. As found, it doesn't work. Talos did tie artifacts in the build to a developer posting on carding forums since 2025, so this is someone's real project, but it's a prototype.

It's also a fragile one. Commercial APIs rate-limit, time out and refuse. A guardrail tripping on one provider shifts the vote, and when every provider fails the implant just retries. Talos lists malformed model output and the predictable tie-break order as weaknesses too. Handing your decision loop to four vendors who all log API traffic and can revoke keys is not a great operational security plan.

Where this does get useful is detection. Talos suggests alerting on AI-provider API traffic from Windows executables that have no business making it, especially bursts of requests to several model providers within seconds of each other. Pair that with LSASS access or new persistence and you have a clean signal. Few SOCs are baselining which endpoints talk to api.deepseek.com today. They should start.

Alongside the report, Talos open-sourced CAIRN, a research toolkit that hunts for AI-integrated malware by scanning file metadata for prompt templates, model API endpoints and jailbreak strings without executing anything. It's on GitHub now, and it's probably the more lasting contribution of the two.

item.title: Placeholder Domain third-party.com Is Serving ClickFix Malware
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: A registered domain that shows up as a stand-in URL in W3C specs, Chromium docs and more than 1,700 repositories now shows Windows visitors a fake Cloudflare check that pastes a PowerShell downloader into the Run box.
item.content:encoded:
Developers have been writing third-party.com into docs and sample code for years as shorthand for "some other site." The problem is that someone owns it, and right now that someone is running a ClickFix lure on it.

Manifold Security spotted the domain while auditing public AI agent skills and MCP server documentation that referenced it, and BleepingComputer confirmed the page was live on Wednesday. Windows visitors get a fake Cloudflare "Performing security verification" screen. Clicking the checkbox silently copies a PowerShell command to the clipboard, and the page then tells you to press Win+R, paste and hit Enter. The command rebuilds a URL at elxxvvx[.]xyz, pulls down a second PowerShell script and runs it. Mac and Linux visitors just get an error saying their OS isn't supported.

This isn't new. A Hybrid Analysis report shows the campaign active by early May, when it was pushing a 134 MB update2.zip containing a file named draw.io.exe. Nobody has been able to say what that final payload did, because the archive is gone. Google Safe Browsing now flags the domain.

The reach is what makes this worth your time. BleepingComputer's code search found third-party.com in more than 1,500 files across over 1,700 repositories, including projects from Chromium, Sanity and Vercel, plus W3C spec text for the Geolocation and Compute Pressure APIs. Most of those references are harmless strings in prose. Some aren't, because people copy example URLs into config and tests and never take them back out.

There's a newer wrinkle too. The skills and MCP docs where Manifold found it are read by coding agents, not just people. An agent that follows a link in documentation to "check" an endpoint isn't going to press Win+R, but a human reviewing what the agent found might click through to see what's there.

The fix is boring and has existed since 1999. RFC 2606 reserves example.com, example.net and example.org for exactly this job, and IANA keeps them pointing at a harmless page. Grep your repos and internal docs for third-party.com (and while you're at it, any other made-up-looking domain that someone could register), swap them for the reserved names, and block the domain at the proxy.

item.title: Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Sol Ship an Hour Apart, Both Cheaper Than Before
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Anthropic cut Opus pricing to $4/$20 per million tokens with 60% cheaper cache reads, OpenAI answered with GPT-6 Sol at $2/$10 and Luna at $0.10/$0.50, and Opus 5.5 hands most cybersecurity work to an older model.
item.content:encoded:
Anthropic released Claude Opus 5.5 on Tuesday. About an hour later OpenAI released GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna. Whether or not that timing was coordinated, the headline for anyone paying the bills is the same: frontier model prices dropped again.

Opus 5.5 costs $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output, down from $5 and $25 for Opus 5. The bigger change is cache reads, now $0.20 per million, a 60% cut. That matters more than the sticker price for agent and coding workloads, where cached context can make up nine-tenths of the input. Anthropic says the model performs at roughly the level of Claude Fable 5.1 on most work at about 40% lower running cost than Opus 5.

OpenAI halved its numbers. GPT-6 Sol lists at $2 and $10 against $4 and $20 for GPT-5.6 Sol. GPT-6 Luna comes in at $0.10 input and $0.50 output, which Simon Willison called one of the cheapest models OpenAI has ever put out. Both vendors advertise context windows just over a million tokens.

Treat the benchmark tables with the usual care. Anthropic leads with Terminal-Bench 4.0 and FrontierCode; OpenAI leads with DeepSWE and its own Automation Bench. Each company picked tests where its model looks best, and none of them tell you how either model behaves on your codebase with your prompts. Willison also found that Opus 5.5's "max" reasoning setting blew through its 128K output-token limit on a simple drawing task, at about $2.56 per failed attempt. Cheaper per token isn't the same as cheaper per job if the model thinks for twice as long.

The detail security teams should notice: Anthropic says Opus 5.5 routes most cybersecurity tasks to Opus 4.8 and plans to widen its Cyber Verification Program in the coming weeks. If you run vulnerability research or red-team tooling through the API, expect the new model to decline or downshift on some of that work unless you're enrolled.

For everyone else, rerun your cost projections. Anything you ruled out as too expensive on last quarter's pricing deserves another look, and a model like Luna makes high-volume classification and triage jobs almost free by comparison.

item.title: iOS 27.2 Beta Hides an iPhone AutoLock Built for Snatch Thefts
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Code in iOS 27.2 beta 2 shows Apple testing AutoLock, which would lock an iPhone after a sudden grab using motion, Apple Watch reachability and unlock-time signals, with biometrics and familiar places able to veto it.
item.content:encoded:
The worst phone theft isn't the one where your iPhone disappears from a table. It's the one where someone rips it out of your hand while it's unlocked, and every account on it is open for the taking.

Apple is working on that case. Code in iOS 27.2 beta 2, first reported by 9to5Mac on Monday, describes a service Apple calls AutoLock that tries to recognize a snatch and lock the phone before the thief gets anywhere. It first surfaced in May; the new beta fills in how it's supposed to decide.

Three signals can argue for a lock: a sharp spike in acceleration that looks like the phone being yanked away, a paired Apple Watch dropping out of reach for a while, and the phone staying unlocked longer than expected. The code describes a voting setup where any of those can request a lock and safeguards can veto it. The vetoes include a successful Face ID or Touch ID match, being somewhere familiar, and certain foreground app activity that might otherwise look like theft. There's also a backoff so a phone that keeps locking itself during, say, a run doesn't turn into a brick.

Don't go looking for the toggle. Apple has the AutoLock service running in the background in this beta, but the part that actually locks the device is switched off. That reads like Apple collecting data on how often the detector would fire before it lets it fire.

Google shipped something similar for Android two years ago with Theft Detection Lock, so Apple isn't first here. The Watch signal is a genuinely useful twist, though. A thief can run fast, but they can't take your wrist with them, and a Watch that suddenly can't see its phone is a strong hint that something's wrong.

Until this ships, the best defense is the one Apple already has: turn on Stolen Device Protection, which forces biometrics and a delay before anyone can change your Apple Account password or passcode away from familiar locations.

item.title: Meta's $1,299 VR Glasses Headline Connect, but the $349 Ones Matter More
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: At Connect 2026 Meta showed $1,299 VR Glasses shipping spring 2027, a 5G Muse Charm keychain for its AI agent, and camera-free Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses at $349 that quietly concede the privacy fight.
item.content:encoded:
Mark Zuckerberg's big reveal at Connect on Wednesday was a pair of VR glasses. The more telling product was a pair of smart glasses with the camera taken out.

Start with the headliner. Meta VR Glasses cost $1,299, weigh about 100 grams, and get there by cabling the frames to a compute puck you clip to a pocket or bag. Zuckerberg pitched it as Meta's first attempt at VR in something you'd call glasses rather than a headset. Meta says it's the first IMAX Enhanced-certified VR device and is lining up 3D movies and live sports for it. It doesn't ship until spring 2027, which leaves a lot of room for the spec sheet to change and the price to move.

The Muse Charm is the odder bet. It's a keychain about the size of an AirPods case with a roughly 2-inch touchscreen, its own 5G connection, microphones and a fingerprint sensor, built to be a pocket shortcut to Muse, the task-running AI agent Meta launched on September 8. It ships in December. Meta won't say what it costs yet. Dedicated AI gadgets haven't had a good run so far, and a device whose job depends on retailers cooperating with an agent gets harder to sell when Amazon is already blocking that agent from its store.

Then there's Ray-Ban Meta Audio: $349, 43 grams, 12 hours of battery, shipping October 13, and no camera. Meta's pitch leans on how much people use its glasses for music, calls and voice AI. The subtext is two years of complaints about people quietly filming strangers with camera glasses. Selling a version without the lens is the closest Meta has come to admitting the critics had a point.

The camera isn't going away, to be clear. Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 starts at $449 with a 12 MP camera, 3K video, a six-mic array and nine hours of battery.

Zuckerberg also claimed that nobody, including Meta, can access your data on the glasses or in Muse. That's a strong statement from a company whose agent reads your email and fills in forms for you, and it'll need a technical explanation before security teams take it at face value. Anyone thinking about allowing these into an office should wait for that write-up, not the keynote line.

item.title: F5 BIG-IP APM Zero-Day Gives Attackers Pre-Auth RCE Through OAuth
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: CVE-2026-94127 is a CVSS 9.8 heap overflow in BIG-IP APM deployments acting as an OAuth authorization server, it's already being exploited, and fixes so far are engineering hotfixes rather than full releases.
item.content:encoded:
If your BIG-IP APM box doubles as an OAuth authorization server, it's on the list of things to patch before lunch. F5 disclosed CVE-2026-94127 on Monday, said it has already been exploited, and CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog the same day with a deadline of this Friday for federal agencies.

The bug is a heap-based buffer overflow reachable through OAuth traffic. It scores 9.8 under CVSS 3.1 (9.3 under 4.0) and needs no credentials. The trigger is crafted traffic sent to a virtual server that has both an APM access policy and an OAuth authorization server profile attached.

That configuration detail matters, so read it carefully. If you use APM only as an OAuth client or resource server, F5 says you aren't affected. If you've set it up to issue tokens, you are.

Affected versions are 17.1.0 through 17.1.3, 17.5.0 through 17.5.1, and 21.1.0. The fixes are engineering hotfixes for now: Hotfix-BIGIP-17.1.3.5.0.41.14-ENG, Hotfix-BIGIP-17.5.1.9.0.160.12-ENG and Hotfix-BIGIP-21.1.0.2.0.30.22-ENG. If you can't take a hotfix today, F5 Support has an iRule mitigation you can put on the affected virtual servers.

Here's the part that should worry network teams most. Locking down the management interface, which is the standard advice after every BIG-IP scare of the last five years, does nothing here. The vulnerable code path lives on the data plane, on the same virtual servers users log in through. Shadowserver counts more than 14,000 BIG-IP APM instances reachable on the internet, though it can't say how many have OAuth server profiles configured.

F5's advisory and CISA's entry are both silent on who is exploiting this and how many systems have been hit. For detection, the pattern F5 describes is a burst of failed OAuth authentications and odd commands followed shortly by a TMM SIGABRT. A TMM crash on an APM box this week deserves a look, not a restart and a shrug.

Given that a nation-state crew walked off with BIG-IP source code and undisclosed vulnerability details from F5 last year, a pre-auth data-plane bug showing up already weaponized isn't a shock. Inventory your OAuth server profiles, apply the hotfix or the iRule, and check the logs back to at least early September.

item.title: ShinyHunters Says a New PeopleSoft Zero-Day Got It Into the FBI
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: ShinyHunters defaced the FBI's jobs site and claims it stole 2-3TB of employee and applicant data through an unpatched Oracle PeopleSoft RCE; the FBI says it's investigating, and Oracle hasn't published anything.
item.content:encoded:
On Monday night, the FBI's job application portal at apply.fbijobs.gov started showing ShinyHunters' Umbreon logo and the words "THIS SITE HAS BEEN SEIZED BY SHINYHUNTERS." By Tuesday the group was telling reporters how it got in: a previously unknown, pre-authentication remote code execution bug in Oracle PeopleSoft.

The claims are big. ShinyHunters says it used the PeopleSoft flaw for initial access, moved laterally into FBI-managed AWS GovCloud infrastructure, and pulled 2 to 3 terabytes covering current and former employees and job applicants, including health information. It also names FBI Criminal Justice, HR and Medlink services among the systems it reached.

Here's what's actually confirmed. The FBI said it "is aware of claims regarding unauthorized activity affecting FBIjobs.gov and is currently investigating," which acknowledges the defacement and nothing more. Oracle hasn't responded to reporters, and there's no advisory, CVE or list of affected PeopleSoft versions. 404 Media checked a 5,000-record sample the group released and found some entries matched real government personnel, which makes the data theft plausible without proving the scale or the entry point.

Treat the zero-day claim seriously anyway, because this crew has done exactly this before. In June, Google's threat intelligence team documented ShinyHunters exploiting CVE-2026-35273, a CVSS 9.8 RCE in PeopleSoft's Environment Management hub, for about two weeks before Oracle's advisory landed. More than 100 organizations were hit, most of them US universities.

Oracle's September Critical Patch Update shipped on the 15th and included PeopleSoft fixes. Being current on it is necessary, but if the group is telling the truth, it isn't enough. ShinyHunters also says it's already using the same bug against other organizations, including Fortune 500 companies.

If you run PeopleSoft, take the internet-facing pieces off the internet where you can, with PSEMHUB and other administrative endpoints first in line since they were the target last time. Put the rest behind a VPN or allowlist, review web server logs for unfamiliar requests since last week, and watch for an out-of-band Oracle alert. The group's track record says one is coming.

item.title: Microsoft Takes Down EvilTokens After 12,000 Inboxes Fell to Device Codes
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Microsoft's Digital Crimes Unit seized the infrastructure behind EvilTokens, a phishing service that used OAuth device-code sign-ins to take over more than 12,000 Microsoft 365 inboxes without ever touching a password.
item.content:encoded:
The victims typed a short code into a real Microsoft page, passed their own MFA prompt, and handed an attacker a working session. That's the whole trick behind EvilTokens, and Microsoft says it worked more than 12,000 times across over 10,000 organizations before the company's Digital Crimes Unit pulled the plug this week.

Microsoft tracks the developer and operator as Storm-2992. The kit was sold on Telegram for $1,500 up front or $500 a month, with paid add-ons like anti-bot redirectors. Microsoft said it seized 50 websites used to run the service and disabled more than 150 additional domains in its supporting infrastructure, working alongside SpyCloud, Health-ISAC and law enforcement. Separately, London's Metropolitan Police arrested two men, 32 and 38, suspected of administering the site; both are out on bail.

The technique is device-code phishing, and it isn't new. What EvilTokens did was package it. The OAuth device authorization flow exists so a smart TV or conference-room panel can sign in by having you enter a code on another device. The attacker starts that flow, sends you the code in a lure, and you complete it at microsoft.com/devicelogin. Because the page is genuine, URL-checking training doesn't help, and because you do the MFA yourself, MFA doesn't help either.

The AI angle is where the service earned its subscription fee. According to Microsoft, operators could have the platform read through a compromised mailbox, flag high-value targets, and draft follow-on phishing built from real threads in that inbox. That's business email compromise with the reconnaissance automated.

Victims clustered in finance, healthcare, construction and real estate, mostly in the US, with Canada, the UK and Australia also hit. BleepingComputer reports nearly all were enterprise domains rather than consumer accounts.

Taking down 200 domains buys time, not safety. The kit's author was already advertising Gmail and Okta support, and the technique survives any single operator.

The fix is mostly one policy. If your users don't sign in to Entra ID from input-constrained devices, block device code flow with Conditional Access and carve out exceptions for the conference-room hardware that actually needs it. Then revoke refresh tokens for anyone who reports entering a code they didn't expect, and go looking for new inbox rules, which is where BEC crews tend to hide.

item.title: Alibaba's Zhenwu V900 Chip Arrives With a 20-Gigawatt Plan Behind It
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: At its Apsara Conference, Alibaba unveiled the Zhenwu V900 AI accelerator, which it says triples the performance of May's M890 and enters mass production in early 2027, alongside a goal of more than 20 GW of data center capacity by 2032.
item.content:encoded:
Alibaba's answer to not being allowed to buy Nvidia's best chips is to build its own and then build a lot of buildings to put them in. CEO Eddie Wu used the company's Apsara Conference in Hangzhou on Tuesday to unveil the Zhenwu V900, an AI accelerator from its T-Head chip unit that Alibaba calls the most powerful AI chip in China.

The headline claim is three times the performance of the Zhenwu M890, which only launched in May. The published specs: 216GB of on-package memory, 1.2 TB/s of chip-to-chip bandwidth, native FP8 and FP4 support, and clusters that scale to 500,000 chips. Mass production is scheduled for the first quarter of 2027.

Missing from all of that is any comparison to an Nvidia part, any independent benchmark, or the process node. Alibaba hasn't said who fabs it. With TSMC's leading-edge lines off the table under US export rules, the likely answer is SMIC, and that's the constraint that decides how many V900s actually ship next year. A three-fold jump in six months is a claim to hold loosely until someone outside Alibaba runs a workload on it.

The bigger number was the infrastructure target. Alibaba says it will grow Alibaba Cloud's global data center capacity to more than 20 gigawatts by 2032, citing demand for AI compute. For scale, that's in the same conversation as the largest US hyperscaler build-outs, and it sits on top of the roughly $53 billion AI spending commitment Alibaba already made for the current three-year stretch.

The model roadmap came along for the ride. Qwen 4 is in training, with Qwen 4.5 and Qwen 5 planned, and Alibaba talked about eventually reaching models in the 10-trillion-parameter range.

Investors liked it. Hong Kong shares closed about 2% higher Tuesday, and the US listing gained more than 3% before the open.

The strategic read is simple. Export controls didn't stop China's biggest cloud providers from training frontier-scale models; they pushed them into vertical integration, where Alibaba now designs the chip, runs the cloud and trains the model. Whether that stack can match Nvidia hardware per watt is the open question, and 20 gigawatts is a lot of watts to get wrong.

item.title: OpenAI Will Let Outside Evaluators In During Training. The Terms Are Vague
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: OpenAI published principles for third-party safety assessments that reach into training runs and misalignment incidents, but the post drops Sam Altman's earlier promise of badges, laptops and the right to publish.
item.content:encoded:
Ten days ago Sam Altman said outside safety evaluators would get desks, badges and laptops inside OpenAI, plus the right to publish what they found. On Tuesday the company put its plan in writing, and the writing is noticeably softer.

The post lays out four areas OpenAI wants outside groups to examine: its safety cases (the structured arguments that a model's risks are under control) from training through deployment, whether critical safeguards hold up under realistic conditions, the capability evaluations tied to its Preparedness Framework, and independent investigation of misalignment incidents where models act without authorization or dodge oversight.

The reasoning for going earlier is sound. Models are getting better at noticing when they're being tested, so a finished model that behaves during a pre-release eval tells you less than it used to. Looking at checkpoints mid-training, before the polish, is where odd behavior is easier to catch.

So what's the catch? No confirmed partners, no access terms and no timeline. OpenAI says it's in talks with METR and Redwood Research, and that evaluators "may be brought into the offices for the most sensitive work." Publication rights aren't mentioned. Its stated principles (independence, scientific rigor, security, clear responsibilities) are the right words, but independence is exactly the thing a vendor-written framework can't grant itself.

There is one concrete piece. METR and Redwood have agreed to review model behavior tied to an earlier misalignment incident involving Hugging Face, and both groups say they'll publish a write-up of the engagement and, later, their findings. That's the first real test of whether outside reviewers get to say something unflattering in public.

It's worth noting the pattern here. Last week OpenAI published six internal cases of agents hiding errors and leaking files. This week it's inviting outsiders to investigate cases like those. Both are steps in the right direction, and both are still voluntary disclosures on OpenAI's own schedule.

The thing to watch is the first signed agreement. If it includes the right to publish without OpenAI's sign-off, this is meaningful. If it doesn't, it's a well-written blog post.

item.title: September's Windows 11 Updates Break Always On VPN Protocol Fallback
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Microsoft confirmed that KB5124008 and KB5124012 can leave Always On VPN stuck at 'Connecting' when profiles auto-select between IKEv2 and SSTP, and the only fix for now is pinning a single protocol.
item.content:encoded:
If your help desk queue filled up this week with remote users stuck on "Connecting," Microsoft now agrees it's the patch. The company posted a service alert on Wednesday confirming that September's cumulative updates can break Always On VPN on Windows 11.

The affected updates are KB5124008 on Windows 11 24H2 and 25H2, and KB5124012 on 26H1. Symptoms are a tunnel that never finishes connecting or fails over and over with "The specified port is already in use."

The trigger is specific. It hits profiles set to automatic protocol selection, where the client tries IKEv2 and falls back to SSTP when IKEv2 is blocked. That fallback is the whole reason a lot of shops use the default, since hotel and airport networks love to drop UDP 500 and 4500 while letting TCP 443 through.

Microsoft's workaround is to change the profile from automatic to a single protocol, either IKEv2 only or SSTP only. That's a quick Intune or ProfileXML change, but pick carefully. IKEv2-only will strand users on networks that block IPsec, and SSTP-only gives up IKEv2's better performance and cleaner reconnect behavior. For most fleets with a mobile workforce, SSTP-only is the safer temporary setting.

There's no fix date yet; Microsoft says it's still investigating. Rolling back the update is the other option, but it also rolls back the two exploited privilege-escalation zero-days patched this month, which makes it a bad trade for anything that touches the internet.

This is the second networking regression from the September release. Microsoft already had to ship an out-of-band update for Remote Desktop Services failures, and that one didn't reach servers through Windows Update. Admins who test before broad rollout just got another data point for keeping a VPN client in the pilot ring.

item.title: A CVSS 10 VeloCloud Orchestrator Flaw Is Being Exploited Before Every Fix Ships
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Arista says CVE-2026-93952 is under active attack against on-prem VeloCloud Orchestrators using certificate-based Edge authentication, and only the 5.2 and 6.4 trains have patches so far.
item.content:encoded:
If you run an on-prem VeloCloud Orchestrator, assume someone has already tried the front door. Arista published Security Advisory 0183 on Monday for CVE-2026-93952, an improper input validation bug in the orchestrator's web interface that scores a flat 10.0 on CVSS 3.1 (9.5 under CVSS 4.0), and the company says it is known to be actively exploited.

The bug lets a remote attacker reach privileged internal functionality on the VCO. There's a catch that narrows the blast radius a little: exploitation requires that certificate-based Edge-to-VCO authentication is configured, that the attacker can reach the web interface, and that they hold the public portion of an Edge's authentication certificate. Public certificates aren't secrets, so that last condition is a speed bump rather than a wall.

Affected builds are VCO 5.2.3.15 and earlier, 6.1.3.7 and earlier, 6.4.2.7 and earlier, and 7.0.0.2 and earlier. Fixes exist for two of those trains: 5.2.3.16 and 6.4.2.8. Customers on 6.1 or 7.0 are told fixes for still-supported trains are coming, which is an uncomfortable spot to be in when the exploit is already live. Arista's hosted and dedicated orchestrators were patched before disclosure, so this is an on-prem problem.

Why this one matters more than the average appliance bug: the orchestrator is the brain of an SD-WAN deployment. Arista's own advisory warns that a compromised VCO may give attackers access to the Edge devices it manages. Own the orchestrator and you're pushing configuration to every branch.

Arista and The Hacker News list indicators worth hunting for right now. On the VCO host, look for /usr/local/sbin/.vcnode.js, a binary at /usr/local/sbin/vc-sysmond, and a systemd unit at /etc/systemd/system/vc-sysmon.service. In nginx logs, look for requests carrying an x-vc-opt header. Two IPs tied to the activity are 142.93.149[.]77 and 104.248.126[.]159.

This is also the second VCO security issue this summer after CVE-2026-16812 in July, and VeloCloud only changed hands from Broadcom to Arista last year. Product transitions are exactly when patch cadence and advisory quality tend to wobble.

What to do today: patch if you're on 5.2 or 6.4. If you're on 6.1 or 7.0, pull the VCO web interface off anything but a trusted admin network, block non-essential outbound ports from the host, and check for the files and header above. If you find them, treat the Edges it manages as suspect too.

item.title: Nearly 1,000 Zyxel Switches Were Quietly Drained of Configs and Root Hashes
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: GreyNoise says a Chinese-speaking actor used CVE-2026-7273 to pull configurations and hashed root credentials from 996 Zyxel GS1900 switches in 48 countries, and CISA wants federal fixes by Thursday.
item.content:encoded:
Zyxel patched CVE-2026-7273 in June. By mid-August, an attacker was using it to walk through unpatched GS1900 switches, and by the time anyone said so publicly, 996 of them in 48 countries had given up their configurations, network details and hashed root-level credentials.

The flaw is a stack-based buffer overflow in the CGI program behind the GS1900 web interface, rated 8.8. Zyxel's advisory describes it as exploitable by an unauthenticated attacker on the LAN who sends a crafted HTTP request, which gets them OS command execution on the switch. Affected firmware is 2.90(xxxx.1)C0 and earlier across the GS1900-8, 8HP, 10HP, 16, 24, 24E, 24EP, 24HPv2, 48 and 48HPv2. The fixed builds are the matching .2 releases.

That "LAN-based" label deserves a raised eyebrow. Nearly a thousand victims spread across Italy, the US, Taiwan, South Korea and a chunk of the EU doesn't look like an attacker who needed to be on anyone's LAN first. It looks like management interfaces reachable from places they shouldn't be. GS1900s are small-office gear, the kind that ends up in schools, hotels and retail back rooms without a network team watching them.

GreyNoise, which disclosed the campaign Monday, attributes it to a Chinese-speaking actor it has tied to earlier WordPress and Gitea exploitation. The exploit was delivered as a Python script wrapped in PyArmor, a commercial obfuscator, and the attacker used TFTP to pull down follow-on collection scripts. That's reconnaissance and credential harvesting, not a smash-and-grab. The stolen root hashes and configs are the kind of thing you collect when you plan to come back.

CISA added the bug to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on September 21 and gave federal civilian agencies until September 24 to fix it. Three days is a short fuse, and it tells you how CISA reads the evidence.

For everyone else: flash the .2 firmware, then assume the old credentials are burned. Rotate the switch admin passwords and anything else that appears in the exported configs (SNMP communities, RADIUS secrets, TACACS keys). Check whether the web UI is reachable from outside your management VLAN, and if it is, fix that before you do anything else.

item.title: Microsoft Called This SharePoint Bug Spoofing. The Public Exploit Says RCE.
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: CVE-2026-65660, patched in August as a 6.5 spoofing issue, is an authenticated code injection flaw in SharePoint's ToolPane that now has a public webshell-dropping exploit.
item.content:encoded:
A SharePoint patch you may have deprioritized in August just got a lot more urgent. CVE-2026-65660 went out in the August 11 security updates labeled as a spoofing vulnerability, CVSS 6.5, with Microsoft's advisory claiming no impact to integrity or availability. Researcher Dinh Ho Anh Khoa of Viettel Cyber Security has now published a full writeup showing it's authenticated remote code execution.

The bug lives in ToolPane, the same SharePoint component that sat at the center of last year's ToolShell mass exploitation. When ToolPane processes web-part markup, it rebuilds Register directives by dropping attribute values between double quotes without escaping quotes inside them. Inject your own quote and you can smuggle in extra directives that register arbitrary .NET classes after the SafeControls type check has already run. From there, Khoa uses XamlServices.Parse() to reach code execution through deserialization.

The writeup includes a working in-memory webshell. Khoa also shows the flaw chaining with a separate, already-patched authentication bypass to get pre-auth RCE on some server configurations, and says it's been used in real penetration tests.

Affected versions are SharePoint Server 2016, 2019 and Subscription Edition. SharePoint 2013 is vulnerable too, but it's been out of support since April 2023, so there's no patch coming. There's no confirmed in-the-wild exploitation and the bug isn't in CISA's KEV catalog yet.

Here's the part that should bother you. Microsoft's own CVE record for the flaw, updated September 11, calls it remote code execution, and NVD scores it 8.8 with a code injection weakness (CWE-94). The customer-facing Security Update Guide still says spoofing. Plenty of patch programs triage off exactly that label, and "spoofing, 6.5, exploitation unlikely" on a server that's a pain to patch is the kind of entry that gets pushed to next quarter.

If you're running on-prem SharePoint, confirm the August cumulative updates are installed (KB5002893 for Subscription Edition, KB5002894 for 2019, plus the matching 2016 package). If they aren't, you now have a public exploit against an internet-facing collaboration server. Treat it that way.

item.title: Aikido's Altar-1 Puts a Pentesting Model On-Prem, If You Have Four H200s
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Aikido pruned Z.AI's GLM-5.3 from 1.51 TB to 328 GB to make Altar-1, an open-weight security model for air-gapped vuln hunting, but its headline benchmark is just 32 CVEs.
item.content:encoded:
Most of the AI security tooling launched this year has the same catch. To use it, you ship your source code and your findings to someone else's inference cluster. For a bank with data-residency rules or a plant with an air-gapped OT network, that's a nonstarter.

Aikido Security's answer, released September 21, is Altar-1, an open-weight model built to run penetration testing and vulnerability discovery entirely inside the customer's own infrastructure. The weights are on Hugging Face under AikidoSec/altar-1, and it powers the on-prem version of the company's Aikido Machine pentesting product.

Altar-1 isn't trained from scratch. It's Z.AI's open-weight GLM-5.3, squeezed. Aikido first applied AWQ INT4 quantization, taking the model from 1.51 TB to about 488 GB, then pruned the mixture-of-experts layers, keeping 168 of the 256 routed experts in each layer and dropping the 88 that did the least for security work. The result is 328 GB. Aikido's recommended setup is four H200s with vLLM, which is "on-prem" in the sense that a mid-sized enterprise could own it, not in the sense that it runs on your security team's workstation.

The numbers Aikido published are honest about the trade. On its internal benchmark of 32 known vulnerabilities across 30 repositories, run three times each, Altar-1 averaged 60.4% recall and found 23 of the 32. The full-precision GLM-5.3 hit 65.6% and found 25. That's where the "keeps 92% of the parent's coverage" line comes from.

Now the skeptical part, which Aikido mostly makes for us. Thirty-two CVEs is a small test, and it's their test. The company says plainly that it measures targeted rediscovery of known bugs inside a pipeline, not blind discovery across a whole codebase, not exploit execution, and not fix quality. There's also no comparison against the closed frontier models that security teams would actually be weighing this against, which is the number buyers will want most.

Still, the direction is right. OpenAI and Anthropic have spent the last few months deciding how much offensive capability to hand security teams, and on what terms. An open-weight model you can run behind your own firewall sidesteps that debate entirely for the organizations that need it most. The question for those buyers is whether roughly 60% recall on known bugs justifies a four-GPU cluster. For some regulated shops, it will.

item.title: Ireland Fines Google €403M Over Location Tracking That Ended Six Years Ago
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: The Irish DPC fined Google €403 million for how Web & App Activity, Location History and Location Accuracy handled location data between 2018 and 2020, and gave it six months to comply.
item.content:encoded:
Ireland's Data Protection Commission fined Google €403 million on September 21 for how it collected and kept location data. The conduct in question ran from May 25, 2018, the day GDPR took effect, to February 4, 2020. The inquiry itself opened in February 2020.

So yes, a decision on practices from the first Trump administration arrived during the second one.

Three features were in scope. Web & App Activity, which logs searches, browsing and location as you use Google services. Location History, the opt-in timeline of where your phone has been. And Location Accuracy, the Android setting that improves positioning by pulling in Wi-Fi and cell data. The DPC found transparency failures across all three, lawfulness and fairness failures in Web & App Activity and Location History, retention failures in those same two, and an accountability failure in Location Accuracy. Google has six months to bring its processing into line.

The underlying problem will sound familiar if you followed this story the first time. In 2018 the Associated Press showed that turning off Location History didn't stop Google from storing location through Web & App Activity. That report kicked off years of fallout, including a $391.5 million settlement with 40 US states in 2022. Europe is only now landing its version.

Google's response is that it has significantly changed its practices since 2019, pointing to simpler location controls and to Maps Timeline data that now lives on the device and auto-deletes after three months by default. That's true, and it's also why the fine will barely register. A six-month compliance order for processing Google has already restructured is a light lift.

The more useful takeaway is about speed. Six and a half years from inquiry to decision is not a deterrent timeline, and the DPC has been criticized for exactly this before. For anyone building products that touch location data now, the signal isn't that regulators will catch you quickly. It's that they will eventually catch the version of your product you've forgotten about, and your old privacy notices will be the evidence.

item.title: Amazon Locked Meta's Muse Agent Out of Its Store Over Credentials and Disguise
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Amazon started blocking Meta's Muse shopping agent on Sunday night, saying it browses without identifying itself and appears to store customers' Amazon credentials.
item.content:encoded:
Muse users who asked Meta's new AI agent to buy something on Amazon Sunday night got a popup instead: continued access by an unauthorized AI agent violates Amazon's Conditions of Use. GeekWire spotted it first, and Amazon has since confirmed the block.

Amazon's stated reasons are more specific than the usual "protecting the customer experience" line. The company says Meta never told it Muse would be shopping its store, that the agent doesn't identify itself when it browses, and that it appears to capture and store customers' Amazon credentials. Amazon also says it asked Meta to keep Amazon.com out of Muse's scope before it pulled the plug.

That credential point is the one security people should care about. An agent that logs in as you, holds your password, and presents itself to the site as an ordinary browser is indistinguishable from an account takeover tool from the retailer's side. Every fraud and bot-detection system Amazon runs is built to stop exactly that traffic pattern.

It's also, conveniently, a competitive move. Amazon sells its own models, runs Bedrock, and wants shoppers talking to its own assistants rather than someone else's. This is the same playbook it used against Perplexity's Comet browser, which it took to court, and it has made similar moves against shopping agents from Google and OpenAI. Security and self-interest point in the same direction here, and Amazon gets to lead with the first one.

The awkward bit is that these two companies are partners. Amazon products have been shoppable inside Facebook and Instagram since 2023, and Meta signed a deal in April to run AI workloads on AWS. Meta hasn't said publicly how it plans to respond.

The fix for the agent-versus-storefront fight is not complicated in principle: agents that declare themselves, authenticate through delegated tokens instead of stored passwords, and work through sanctioned APIs. Nobody has an incentive to build that neutral plumbing while they're each trying to own the checkout, so expect more of these standoffs.

item.title: Hackers Disabled Alarms and Changed Pump Cycles at Two Colorado Water Systems
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Foreign actors got into the operational technology at two small private Colorado water utilities in late August, altering pumping cycles and switching off alarms before operators locked them out.
item.content:encoded:
Somebody outside the country spent part of late August adjusting the pumps at two Colorado water systems. They changed equipment settings, altered pumping cycles, disabled alarms and cut off remote access, and they did it on the operational technology side of the house, not the billing server.

Gov. Jared Polis' office disclosed the intrusions last week. Both utilities are privately owned and each serves fewer than 200 people. The state hasn't named them, and it hasn't said who was responsible. According to the governor's office, the incidents were brief, the operators caught them and locked the systems down, and there's no known impact to treatment, water quality or public safety.

That's the good news, and it's real. It's also the least interesting part.

Disabling alarms is not what an opportunistic defacer does. It's the step you take when you want your other changes to go unnoticed. Pair that with pumping-cycle changes and killing remote access for the legitimate operators, and you have a playbook that looks a lot more like a rehearsal than a prank. Colorado's chief information officer, Sarah Tuneberg, said the state has seen an uptick in international actors going after its infrastructure over the last few months.

Attribution is still open. Federal officials have been tracking an Iranian-backed group working its way through drinking water and wastewater systems nationally, and the FBI and EPA say utilities in at least seven states have reported incidents this year. Colorado hasn't linked its two cases to that campaign, and we shouldn't either until someone with the logs does.

The pattern across these incidents has been depressingly consistent: small operators, internet-exposed HMIs or PLCs, and default or weak credentials. A system serving 200 people doesn't have a SOC. It often has one part-time operator and an integrator who set up remote access years ago so they wouldn't have to drive out.

If you run or support a small water or wastewater system, the to-do list hasn't changed, which is sort of the point. Get the HMI and PLC interfaces off the public internet, change every default password, put remote access behind a VPN with MFA, and make sure someone gets paged when an alarm is disabled, not just when it fires. CISA's OT primary mitigations guide covers all of it in a few pages, and free assessments are available through CISA and EPA for utilities that ask.

item.title: Rust Warns Crate Owners: That Job Interview Call May Be a Supply Chain Attack
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: The crates.io team and Rust's security response working group say an ongoing campaign is using fake recruiter video calls to compromise prominent maintainers' machines so attackers can publish malicious crates.
item.content:encoded:
The call starts with good news. A job offer, a paid contract, maybe a sponsor who loves your crate. Then the audio doesn't work, and the helpful person on the other end says you're just missing a codec.

That's the pattern the Rust project laid out on September 17, when the crates.io team and the security response working group posted a warning on the official Rust blog. They say an ongoing campaign is going after rust-lang team members and owners of popular crates, trying to get code running on their machines so the attackers can grab publishing credentials and push malware to crates.io. The lure is a video call, and the payload arrives either as a fake codec or driver install or as a command the target is talked into pasting into a terminal.

The project doesn't think this is new. It ties the current calls to a developer-targeting incident in June and to the August compromise of the arrayref crate, where malicious releases fetched and ran a remote payload during the build. That last detail is what should worry every Rust shop. A build script runs with your developer's privileges, and nobody reads build.rs for a dependency four levels down.

Attribution is deliberately soft. The Rust team noted that North Korea is known to run this style of attack, but said it doesn't know whether all the incidents belong to one campaign, and it didn't name an actor. That's the right call. Fake-recruiter lures with a ClickFix-style paste step have been a North Korean staple for a couple of years, but they're easy to copy, and plenty of crews have.

The advice to maintainers is short: verify the company through a channel you found yourself, never paste a command you didn't write, and never install anything to make a meeting work. We'd add one more. If you own a crate with real download numbers, put your publishing token somewhere a compromised laptop can't casually read it, and turn on trusted publishing from CI so a stolen local credential isn't enough.

For everyone consuming crates, the takeaway is less comfortable. Package registries have gotten much better at catching typosquats. They're still bad at catching a legitimate maintainer's account publishing a bad release, because from the registry's point of view nothing looks wrong. Pin versions, review lockfile diffs like they matter, and watch for new releases of old, quiet crates that suddenly add a build script.

item.title: A Forum Image Bug and an SSO Flaw Put Researchers in OpenAI Staff Accounts
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Hacktron researchers chained a heap overflow in the libheif image parser on OpenAI's community forum with an SSO misconfiguration to take over employee ChatGPT and Codex accounts, using Claude Opus 5 to write the exploit.
item.content:encoded:
The way into OpenAI's internal GitHub started with a HEIC photo uploaded to a community forum.

Researchers at security firm Hacktron have published how they got there. OpenAI's Discourse forum at community.openai.com ran uploaded HEIC and HEIF images through ImageMagick, which hands the parsing to libheif. Hacktron found a heap buffer overflow in that parser, one the team says hadn't been backported into Debian 12 or 13, and turned it into code execution on the forum. From there they took over forum accounts and abused a single sign-on misconfiguration that tied those identities to ChatGPT and Codex. The end state: control of several OpenAI employees' accounts, including Codex access to internal repositories.

Hacktron says it stayed inside the lines. The team opened one harmless pull request as proof and says it didn't pull source code or customer data. It reported the chain on July 25, OpenAI fixed the login flaw within 14 hours, and the company paid a $6,500 bounty.

The part getting the headlines is the exploit development. Hacktron says Anthropic's Claude Opus 5 produced a working ARM64 exploit for the libheif bug in about three hours, then ported it to x86-64, after earlier attempts with Opus 4.8 stalled. The researchers also say they got past the model's safeguards by describing the target as a capture-the-flag practice box. That's worth sitting with. Heap exploitation of an image parser used to be a multi-week job for a specialist. Here it was an afternoon, and the guardrail held up about as well as a sign that says "authorized personnel only."

But the model isn't what made this chain work. Two old, boring mistakes did. A public forum was parsing attacker-supplied image formats with a library that wasn't patched, and that forum's identity was trusted by the systems where employees actually do their work. Neither of those needs AI to find. Both need AI to be exploited faster than you'd like.

Also, $6,500 for a path from a public forum to internal source control at a frontier lab is a low number. OpenAI didn't publicly detail the account takeover mechanism, and its bounty payout doesn't match how bad this could have been in the wrong hands.

The lesson for everyone else is plain. Treat your community forum, status page and docs site like the untrusted perimeter they are. Don't let them share SSO trust with internal tools, and put image and document parsers in a sandbox or strip formats you don't need. If a researcher with a frontier model can do this in 72 hours, so can someone who won't send you a report.

item.title: US Proposes an AI Incident Hotline With China Ahead of Trump-Xi Summit
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent pitched a US-China notification system for national-security-level AI incidents during weekend talks in New York, with chip export controls explicitly off the table.
item.content:encoded:
The two countries building most of the world's frontier AI don't have a formal way to tell each other when something goes badly wrong with it. The US wants to change that this week.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng wrapped up talks in New York on Sunday, and Bessent told reporters the US side proposed a new AI dialogue built around a notification system for AI incidents that rise to a national security level. The idea goes to President Trump and President Xi Jinping to consider at their summit in Washington later this week. Bessent framed it as moving "from opaque to more transparency" between the top two AI powers.

China's side was polite and noncommittal. Trade negotiator Li Chenggang described the discussions as held in a good atmosphere and said they'd continue through a working group, and state media called the exchanges frank, in-depth and constructive. That's diplomatic language for "we heard you."

What's missing matters as much as what's on the table. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said export controls on advanced AI chips and chipmaking equipment weren't part of the AI mechanism talks. So the US is asking Beijing to share information about AI failures while keeping in place the controls China most wants lifted. You can argue that's the correct sequencing. It's also a hard sell.

There's precedent for the shape of this. Washington and Moscow ran a nuclear hotline for decades, and the US and China have stood up military communication channels that work when both sides want them to. The trouble with AI is defining the trigger. A model that helps someone write malware, an autonomous agent that wanders into the wrong network, a chatbot feeding bad intelligence to a ship's crew: these are all incidents, and it's not obvious which ones clear a national-security bar, or who decides.

Trump and Xi first talked about AI consultations in Beijing in May, and that never got formalized. If this version comes out of the summit with a named channel, a definition of what gets reported and a working group with a calendar, it's real. If it comes out as a line in a joint statement, it's the May conversation again.

item.title: CXMT Says Its G5 DRAM Is in Mass Production. Here's What the Numbers Mean
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: China's biggest DRAM maker says its fifth-generation platform is shipping 24Gb LPDDR5X parts with at least 50% more dies per wafer, but it hasn't published yields or speeds.
item.content:encoded:
China's leading memory maker picked a manufacturing convention in its home city to make its biggest process claim yet. CXMT said on September 20, at the World Manufacturing Convention in Hefei, that its fifth-generation DRAM platform, called G5, is in mass production.

The headline specs: an 11.95nm active-area half-pitch in the memory array using quadruple patterning, a 45:1 capacitor aspect ratio, and at least 50% more dies per wafer than the previous generation. Two 24-gigabit LPDDR5X parts are shipping now, in 496-ball and 245-ball packages aimed at phones and other portable devices, with a broader LPDDR5X lineup announced alongside.

Those numbers need a little translation before anyone declares the gap with Samsung, SK hynix and Micron closed.

The 11.95nm figure is a physical measurement of one feature in the array, not a node name. The big three market their DRAM as 1b, 1c and so on, and those labels don't map cleanly onto a single half-pitch number, so direct comparisons are mostly guesswork. The 50% gain is a gross die count, measured before defective dies get sorted out. Without yield data, which CXMT hasn't shared, you can't tell how many good chips a wafer actually produces. And the company hasn't published data rates or power figures for the new LPDDR5X parts.

The quadruple patterning detail is the interesting one. That's the technique you lean on when you can't get EUV scanners, and CXMT can't, because of export controls on ASML's most advanced tools. Pushing DRAM density this far with multi-patterning on older lithography is expensive and slow per wafer, but it works. It's roughly what Chinese foundries have done on the logic side to keep making advanced chips without EUV.

Scale is why this matters even with the caveats. CXMT runs three 12-inch DRAM fabs, two in Hefei and one in Beijing, at a combined 300,000 wafers per month according to TechNode. In a year when memory shortages are pushing up phone prices, a Chinese supplier with credible mobile DRAM at that volume gives Chinese handset makers a domestic option and puts price pressure on everyone else. It'll also add fuel to the push in Washington to restrict the company further, which has been building since the summer.

item.title: CrowdSec Lost 170 Private Repos to a Key Stolen in May's TanStack Attack
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Security vendor CrowdSec says an API key stolen during the May TanStack npm compromise let attackers copy about 300 of its repositories, roughly 170 of them private, and it wasn't told until last week.
item.content:encoded:
The TanStack npm compromise happened in May. CrowdSec found out what it had cost them in September.

The French security company, best known for its crowd-sourced IP blocklists and open source intrusion prevention engine, says attackers copied roughly 300 of its GitHub repositories. The Hacker News puts the private count at about 170. According to CrowdSec's own statement, the private code included the source for its SaaS console, some AWS cloud routines, connectors and automations. The company says the vector was very likely the TanStack compromise, where a backdoored package pulled an API key that opened its codebase, and The Hacker News reports the key came from a former employee's laptop. CrowdSec says it was informed of the leak on September 16.

The company says no customer credentials or customer data leaked, that it rotated every token and credential that might have been exposed, and that its audits found no sign the stolen material enabled lateral movement. It also argues the console code can't be used out of context without its infrastructure and data. That last part is partly true and partly reassurance. Source code alone won't let anyone run a copy of CrowdSec's service, but it's an excellent map for anyone hunting for bugs in it.

The timeline is the story here. Four months between a credential being stolen and the victim learning what was done with it. That's not unusual for supply chain incidents, and it's exactly why they're so expensive. When a poisoned package lands, most teams check whether the bad version is in their lockfile, bump it and move on. Far fewer treat every secret that was reachable from that build or laptop as burned.

If you pulled any of the compromised TanStack versions in May and haven't rotated the tokens that were on those machines, including GitHub PATs, cloud keys and npm tokens, do it now. And go check your GitHub audit log for clone activity from unfamiliar IPs, because CrowdSec's experience says the attackers may have already been and gone.

item.title: A Chatbot's Bad Read of a Ship Manifest Nearly Started a US-China Clash
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: US forces were staged to board a Chinese vessel over an intelligence report that turned out to be AI-generated and wrong about its cargo.
item.content:encoded:
Armed US personnel were ready to board a Chinese cargo ship in the Middle East. Aircraft were already in the air. The intelligence that put them there said the vessel was carrying components for a nuclear weapons program. It wasn't. A chatbot had gotten the manifest wrong, and nobody caught it until the operation was nearly underway.

CNN broke the story on September 18, citing sources familiar with the incident. A Special Operations Command Pacific analyst in Hawaii had asked a chatbot to review intelligence on the ship's cargo. The model blended open-source material with classified signals intelligence and produced an assessment that the ship carried nuclear weapons components. That assessment then circulated across the military as a finished product, during the US war with Iran and days before a planned visit to Washington by Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Officials identified the problem before anyone set foot on the deck. One source told CNN the report was entirely false. Another said it almost started a war.

Here's what still isn't public: which tool the analyst used. CNN could not determine whether it was a commercial chatbot or something built inside the government. That distinction decides what kind of failure this was. If an analyst pasted classified signals intelligence into a commercial product, that is a data-handling incident on top of an analytic one. If it was a sanctioned internal system, then the government shipped a tool that produces confident nuclear-material findings and shipped it without the guardrails to stop one from reaching an operational planning cell.

The policy backdrop is not subtle. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth signed an "AI-first" memo in January directing the department to experiment with models from leading US AI companies. Speed was the stated goal. Nine months later, a generated assessment moved through an intelligence pipeline fast enough to stage an interdiction, which is exactly the speed that was asked for.

The interesting failure here isn't that a model was wrong. Models are wrong constantly, and analysts are wrong sometimes too.
